title: YouTube 20: 6 People Who Found a Fortune by Accident
_sources:
Sources (checked 2026-11-27):
- Cimabue "The Mocking of Christ": Wikipedia "The Mocking of Christ (Cimabue)" (house near Compiegne, 2019, hung above the hotplate, owner in her nineties,
  thought it an old religious icon of little value, 25.8 x 20.3 cm, c. 1280, auctioneer Philomene Wolf noticed it, Eric Turquin attributed it, sold 27 Oct 2019 at
  Acteon Senlis, EUR 24 million with fees, export ban, acquired by the Louvre Nov 2023); Irish Times 27 Oct 2019 ("hung for decades above a cooking hotplate",
  "simply an old icon from Russia", 26 x 20 cm, over EUR 24 million); The Art Newspaper 6 Nov 2023 (Louvre, EUR 24.1m).
- Caravaggio "Judith Beheading Holofernes" (Toulouse): The Art Newspaper 1 Mar 2019 timeline (April 2014 auctioneer Marc Labarbe called to a house in Toulouse,
  Eric Turquin, national treasure, 30-month export ban); artnet News June 2019 ("dark, cluttered, leaky attic", estimate EUR 100-150 million, auction 27 June 2019
  cancelled at the eleventh hour, sold privately, buyer and price confidential, some experts doubt the attribution); Wikipedia (undisclosed amount).
- Hoxne Hoard: Wikipedia "Hoxne Hoard" (16 Nov 1992, farmer Peter Whatling lost a hammer, friend Eric Lawes with metal detector, notified police without digging
  further, archaeologists excavated next day, 14,865 Roman coins: 569 gold, 14,272 silver, 24 bronze, ~200 items of tableware and jewellery, buried after AD 407,
  valued GBP 1.75 million paid to Lawes and shared with Whatling, hammer also recovered and given to the British Museum); Smithsonian Magazine 2017.
- Saddle Ridge Hoard: Wikipedia "Saddle Ridge Hoard" (Feb 2013, couple "John and Mary" walking their dog on their property in Northern California, rusty can
  poking out of the ground, 8 cans, 1,427 gold coins dated 1847-1894, face value $27,980, hid them in an old cooler under a woodpile, Mint-theft theory ruled out);
  NPR 26 Feb 2014 (Sierra Nevada property, Kagin's: about $10 million).
- Declaration of Independence (Adamstown): Snopes; Philadelphia Inquirer (1991, reprint 2009: bought a painting for $4 because he liked the frame, folded document
  between painting and backing); History.com (1989, Adamstown, Pennsylvania, printed by John Dunlap); Christian Science Monitor 3 Jul 2000 (sold 1991 for $2.42 million,
  2000 for about $8.1 million to TV producer Norman Lear and a partner).
- "Tenner" diamond: Sotheby's editorial (late 1980s, car boot sale in Isleworth, West London, haggled from GBP 12 to GBP 10, thought it was costume jewellery,
  wore it regularly, appraised in 2017, cushion-cut 26.27 carats, 19th century); ITV News 7 Jun 2017 (estimate GBP 250,000-350,000, sold at Sotheby's London for GBP 656,750).

lines.text: For decades, this tiny painting hung above a hot plate in an old woman's kitchen. She thought it was worthless.
Then someone took a closer look. A few months later, it sold for twenty-four million euros.
That's number one on this list. But first, five other people who found a fortune completely by accident.
A ring from a car boot sale. A four-dollar painting. A rusty can. A lost hammer. And a leaky attic.
Number six. West London, the late 1980s.
A woman is browsing a car boot sale. That's like a flea market, out of the trunks of cars.
In a box of cheap costume jewelry, she spots a big, sparkly ring. The seller wants twelve pounds. She haggles him down to ten.
She thinks it's glass. So she just wears it. For about thirty years.
Then, in 2017, she finally asks a jeweler to take a look.
It's not glass. It's a real diamond, over twenty-six carats, from the eighteen-hundreds.
Sotheby's expected up to three hundred and fifty thousand pounds.
It sold for six hundred and fifty-six thousand pounds. Not bad for a tenner.
Number five. Adamstown, Pennsylvania, 1989.
A man at a flea market buys an old painting for four dollars. He doesn't care about the picture. He just wants the frame.
At home, he takes it apart. The old frame falls to pieces.
And hidden behind the painting, he finds a folded piece of paper.
It's a copy of the Declaration of Independence. Not a souvenir. One of the very first printings, from July 1776.
Only a couple of dozen copies of that printing were known to still exist.
In 1991, it sold at auction for two point four million dollars.
And nine years later, it sold again. This time for more than eight million.
Number four. Northern California, 2013.
A couple is walking their dog on their own land.
Then, they notice an old rusty can, sticking out of the ground.
They dig it out. Inside: gold coins.
They keep digging. In the end, they find eight cans, with fourteen hundred and twenty-seven gold coins.
The coins are from 1847 to 1894, most of them minted in San Francisco. Their face value: about twenty-eight thousand dollars.
But to collectors, they're worth around ten million.
Some people guessed they were stolen from the San Francisco Mint in 1901. But the Mint said it found no link.
At first, the couple hid them in an old cooler, under a pile of firewood.
And who buried them? To this day, nobody knows.
Number three. Suffolk, England, November 1992.
A farmer loses his hammer somewhere in a field. So he asks a friend for help.
His friend has a metal detector. He got it as a retirement present.
The detector beeps. But it's not the hammer. It's coins. Silver coins. Gold coins. Spoons. Jewelry.
And here's the smart part. He stops digging, and calls the police.
The next day, archaeologists dig out the whole find.
Almost fifteen thousand Roman coins, plus about two hundred silver and gold objects. Buried around sixteen hundred years ago.
It's now in the British Museum. The reward: one point seven five million pounds, shared with the farmer.
Oh, and the hammer? They found that too. It's in the British Museum as well.
Number two. Toulouse, France, 2014.
A family calls a local auctioneer to look at something in their attic. It's dark, cluttered, and the roof is leaking.
Leaning against a wall is a huge, old painting. A woman is cutting off a man's head.
An expert from Paris studies it, and makes a bold claim. He thinks it was painted by Caravaggio, one of the most famous painters of all time.
France bans the painting from leaving the country for more than two years, while experts examine it. Estimates go up to one hundred and fifty million euros.
An auction is set for June 2019. But just days before, it's suddenly called off.
A private collector bought it. The price is a secret. And some experts still doubt it's a real Caravaggio.
And number one. A small town north of Paris, 2019.
A woman in her nineties is selling her house. An auctioneer comes by to value everything inside.
In the kitchen, above the hot plate, hangs a tiny painting on wood. Smaller than a sheet of paper.
The family thinks it's an old religious icon. Nothing special.
But the auctioneer recognizes it right away. It looks like early Italian art. Maybe worth three or four hundred thousand euros.
And the expert who checks it? The same man from the Caravaggio story.
His team scans it with infrared light, and compares it to other works.
The verdict: it's by Cimabue, a master from around 1280. Only a handful of his paintings still exist.
In October 2019, about eight hundred people pack into the auction room. The bids keep climbing.
Twenty-four million euros. For a painting that hung over the stove.
France blocked the buyer from taking it abroad. In 2023, the Louvre bought it.
So maybe go and check what's hanging in your grandma's kitchen.
Which find would you most like to make? Tell me in the comments. And subscribe to Roundhead Stories for more true money stories.
